stories.title: Plea on air fare spikes: Centre informs Supreme Court new rules approved
stories.summary: The Centre on Friday informed the Supreme Court that administrative approval has been granted to rules under the 2024 Act aimed at regulating and controlling India's aviation sector, and is likely to be published in two weeks. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, R Mahadevan and Aparesh Kumar Singh asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to place the published rules under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024 before the court on the next date of hearing. At the outset, Mehta said, "The rules have been finalised and the administrative approval to the rules has been granted. The same would be published within two weeks." The bench posted the matter for hearing on November 16. stories.headline: Supreme Court issues contempt notices to Sanjay Raut, Nikhil Wagle over remarks on CJI
stories.title: Supreme Court issues contempt notices to Sanjay Raut, Nikhil Wagle over remarks on CJI
stories.summary: The bench will consider their explanations before deciding the next steps in proceedings initiated over remarks allegedly undermining judicial authority
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday issued show-cause notices to Shiv Sena (UBT) Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Raut and journalist Nikhil Wagle in criminal contempt proceedings over their public remarks concerning Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and the judiciary.
A bench comprising the CJI and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, however, exempted Raut and Wagle from personal appearance on the next date of hearing, saying it would first consider their explanations.
The show-cause notices were issued on a contempt plea filed by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA).

SCBA President and senior advocate Pradeep Rai alleged that the remarks by Raut and Wagle went beyond the bounds of fair criticism and were capable of undermining public confidence in the Supreme Court.

Expressing concern over statements targeting the judiciary, the CJI observed that courts had consistently upheld personal liberty and fundamental rights, making attacks on the institution particularly unfortunate.
The SCBA pressed for the personal appearance of the respondents.
The bench, however, decided to issue show-cause notices first.
“We are giving a show-cause as of now.
Of course we are granting exemption for personal appearance.
Let us see,” the bench said.
Earlier, Attorney General R Venkataramani had granted consent for initiating criminal contempt proceedings under Section 15(1)(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
The SCBA filed its petition on October 15 and Venkataramani granted consent the same day.

stories.headline: India received 15% below normal monsoon rainfall this year: IMD
stories.title: India received 15% below normal monsoon rainfall this year: IMD
stories.summary: Goa received 196.68 cm rainfall, which is the highest in the country, while Punjab reported 28 cm, the lowest
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India received 76.86 cm rainfall between June 4 and October 15 when the south-west monsoon was active over the country, which is 15 per cent below its long period average of 90.63 cm, according to India Meteorological Department (IMD) data.
The south-west monsoon, after its onset over Keralam on June 4, withdrew from the entire country on October 15.

During this period, except Andaman and Nicobar islands which reported 1 per cent surplus rainfall, all the meteorological sub-divisions in the south peninsula region were deficient with a shortfall between 23 per cent and 46 per cent.
As the north-east monsoon has now set in, these sub-divisions look forward to getting some rains to help the crops in winter season, particularly in non-irrigated areas.
In Central India where monsoon rainfall was 6 per cent below normal, except Maharashtra and Goa, which were deficient, all other states had either normal or excess rainfall.
Maharashtra has reported 23 per cent deficit and Goa 36 per cent.
On the other hand, Odisha received 23 per cent surplus rains, whereas Chhattisgarh 2 per cent shortfall.
Madhya Pradesh had 7 per cent deficit and Gujarat 12 per cent below normal.
The north-west India too received 6 per cent below normal rains like Central India.

Among the major agricultural states in this region, Punjab (-37 per cent), Haryana (-21 per cent) and Rajasthan (-24 per cent) reported deficient rainfall while Uttar Pradesh (+6 per cent) had normal precipitation.
The east and north-east region was 27 per cent deficient as Arunachal Pradesh (-45 per cent), Assam (-29 per cent), Bihar (-32 per cent) and Meghalaya (-61 per cent) had less rainfall.
But, West Bengal has reported 2 per cent deficit and Jharkhand 6 per cent deficit rainfall between June 4 and October 15.

stories.headline: Kashmir Syncretic Traditions
stories.title: Kashmir Syncretic Traditions
stories.summary: Since time immemorial, Kashmir has been the abode of many deities, Sufi saints, seers, and savants of very high spiritual splendour, intensity, and grace who enriched the culture and thought process of the people. The land has been blessed by deities Lord Shiva, Parvati, Brahma, Vishnu, Lord Ram, Sita, and Lord Krishna. Sufi saints and Rishis Lal Ded, Nund Rishi, Shah Hamdani, and Sayed Sharaf-ud-Din Rehman (Bulbul Shah) advocated the oneness of God and brotherhood through divine preachings. Kashmir has also been blessed by the Sikh Gurus, Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, and Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, who also carried the same message. Buddhist monastic Guru Padmasambhav also preached in Kashmir. These noble men believed in the magnanimity of God and spread the message of universal brotherhood. Rishi Kashyap bifurcated a mountain at village Khadniyar, Baramulla, and drained Lake Sati Sar, and as a result, the Valley emerged. The Valley experiences picturesque frames in various seasons, each having its exquisite aroma. God has sanctified all the beauty of nature in the Valley, and Kashmir is indeed the Divine Land, whose beauty takes heavenly shades, from blooming spring flowers to golden autumn leaves. Kashmir, also in all its feminine beauty of crystal -clear streams and lakes, lush green valleys, and magnificent snow-capped Himalayan peaks, qualifies for the title “Paradise on Earth.” Sanskrit poet Kalidasa has written about the Valley: “The place is more beautiful than heaven and is the benefactor of Supreme bliss and happiness. It seems to me that I am taking a bath in the lake of Nectar.” Kashmir has the distinction of being home to many revered Islamic shrines, ancient Hindu temples, and historical Sikh Gurdwaras that reflect a rich example of spiritual harmony. Syncretic traditions are cultural, religious, architectural, and philosophical practices that blend different and distinct belief systems into a new, unified whole. The history of Kashmir is not adequately understood through the background of any particular religion. It is rather the history of a civilization repeatedly shaped over many centuries. The Kashmir Valley became a meeting ground of religious traditions, philosophical systems, languages, political cultures, and social practices. Brahminical traditions, Buddhism, Kashmir Shaivism, Islam, Sufism, Rishism, and later Sikh and Dogra influences did not suddenly appear one after another and disappear. They interacted with what already existed. Elements were absorbed, transformed, resisted, adapted, and sometimes rejected. Once Islam became indigenous to Kashmir, it itself underwent transformation through its encounter with the same local cultural environment. That is where Sufism and, particularly, the Rishi traditions became central. Sayed Ali Hamdani was the greatest missionary, whose personality wielded the most extraordinary influence in the spread of Islam. Sikhism did not become a demographic equivalent o f Islam or the older Hindu traditions of Kashmir, but Sikh institutions, communities, and political authority became part of Kashmir’s evolving social landscape. During the Dogra rule, the political structure changed, administrative institutions changed, and relations among religious communities acquired a new political dimension. The celestial Valley, cradled in its arms, a unique type of Hindu Mysticism and Muslim Sufism. Mysticism in Kashmir was always different; there were Hindu mystics whose principles and methods resembled or were identical to those of Muslim saints. Also, there had been Muslim Rishis who were influenced by Kashmir Shaivism and Hindu thought. Four major Sufi “Silsilas” or orders that obtained prominence between the 12th and 16th centuries were: • Qadiri Order, founded by Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad • Suharwardiya Order, founded by Shihab-al-Din Suharwardi of Persia • Shadhiliya Order, founded by Abu -al-Hasan-al-Shadhili, a Moroccan scholar • Mevlevi Order, founded by Jalal -al-Din Muhammad Rumi, resident of Wakhsh, present-day Tajikistan Another faith that evolved was Rishism. A Rishi is a sage who sees spiritual truth. Abul Fazal writes, “The most respected class of people in this country, Kashmir, is the Rishis.” Although they have not abandoned the traditional and customary form of Taqlid (following), yet they are true in their worship. Emperor Jahangir wrote, “Although they have not acquired learning and Marifa, they live a frank and unostentatious life.” The Islamic philosophy of divine unity of being (Wahdat -ul-Wujud) is not different from Hindu philosophy of non -duality (Advaita). It is not at all surprising that the Rishis constantly preached complete harmony amongst different religions and peace and understanding among their followers. If Lal Ded represents the pre-Islamic spiritual inheritance of Kashmir, Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani (Nund Rishi) represents the extraordinary localisation of Islam. Linguistic syncretism connects people and ideas. Language is the core text of human life that lets us shape thoughts, build societies, and pass down knowledge across time. All faiths in Kashmir, over the entire spectrum of time, spoke the same language, “Koshur.” The Muslim and Hindu communities wore the same dress, “Pheran,” shared common surnames, had some common wedding rituals like the use of Mehendi (Henna), and referred to the bride and groom as Maharein and Mahraz. The communities together engaged in the same music and dance (Rouf, Chakri, Band Pathar). Sufi Mystical Music of Kashmir (SAMA) forms an essential part of the region’s rich mystic and classical traditions called Sufiana Kalam. The lyrics used include Hamd (Praise of God), Na’d (Cosmic sound or Divine Vibration), and mystical poetry of Kashmiri saints. The main instruments used are Santoor, Rubab, and Trumbkanari. Hindus and Muslims together participated in many religious functions. Zain -ul- Abdin participated in the festival of Vyeth Truva (ceremony marking the birth of River Jhelum). Historically, both communities carried out shrine veneration and frequented shrines of Sufi mystics and Rishis, blending Vedantic/Shaivite philosophy with Islamic Sufism. The day after the festival of Herath (Mahashivratri), Muslim neighbours traditionally visited Pandit households to offer greetings and exchange pleasantries (a custom named SALAM), symbolising communal harmony. During the Afghan rule, Jabbar Khan wanted to test the local belief that on Shivratri there is a likelihood of snowfall. He banned the celebration in the scheduled month of February and forced the community to hold it in June/July. To his shock and dismay, it snowed in the Valley on that summer day. The architectural fusion of Kashmir not only represents the adaptation of Islamic principles to local conditions but also underscores the spirit of tolerance and coexistence that has historically defined Kashmiri society. Some of the shrines, often built in a combination of Islamic and Hindu architectural styles, stand as symbols of the harmony that the Rishis sought to create in Kashmir. The wooden structure of Khanqah, adorned with intricate papier-mâché work, colourful floral motifs, and stunning wood carving, as also the magnificent Jama Masjid, are the finest examples of Syncretic Kashmiri Islamic Architecture. The indigenous secularism, traditional composite culture, and social ethos of Kashmir represented communal harmony, religious tolerance, and shared heritage among its people. Though presently people connect with the word Kashmiriyat, this word does not find mention in any important historical accounts. It was sometime in 1975, after the Kashmir Accord, that Mohd Amin (Ibn Mahjoor) had proposed that we must support a political party that is rooted in Kashmir and would retain the culture of Kashmir, and that would be Kashmiriyat. Kashmiriyat and the composite culture got threatened during the armed militancy when the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits took place on 19 January. The word Kashmiriyat has often been quoted in various debates and conferences. Kashmiris have always resisted external aggression that started with the invasion by the Mughals, but what has been more painful is that the nefarious designs during militancy were not understood. With the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits, Kashmiryat and composite culture have taken a huge hit, but all-out efforts are being taken to see to it that this cementing force is not threatened anymore. The militancy in Kashmir affected people of every faith, and tens of thousands of innocent lives were lost. More than 150 Hindu shrines across the Valley were damaged, desecrated, or left in ruins. The terrorist strikes in the Valley did not even spare holy shrines. Foreign terrorist Mast Gul and his men established a retreat near the holy Charar -e-Sharif shrine. The siege lasted for more than 60 days. The siege ended on 11 May 1995 with a fire that engulfed the shrine. 1990. To conclude, Kashmir’s Syncretic traditions were not created by a proclamation. They emerged gradually from centuries of human interaction. The Valley went through a trying time during the militancy period, and it was these traditions and values that helped Kashmir to emerge a winner, embracing people of all faiths. The manner in which people of all faiths stood by each other in total sync and harmony to fight the floods of 2014 was again a great example of Kashmiryat. Gurdwaras, Mosques, and Temples were open to people of all faiths for food and shelter. The efforts being taken for a dignified and secure return of the Kashmiri Pandits are a welcome step to revive the Syncretic Traditions of Kashmir. (The writer is a former Deputy Assistant Chief of Headquarters Integrated Staff (IT), author, and Social Activist. Feedback: sodhidalbir7777@gmail.com )
